items.question: Learn Node.js
answer_points: Node.js is a JavaScript runtime built on Chrome's V8 engine.
It provides modules for HTTP, file system, and asynchronous I/O.
Key topics include command line usage, HTTP servers, file system operations, async patterns, TypeScript, package management, diagnostics, testing, and security.
Node.js uses an event-driven, non-blocking model.
follow_ups: What are the main use cases for Node.js?
How does Node.js handle asynchronous operations?
items.summary: Overview of Node.js learning resources covering core modules and best practices.

items.question: Getting Started with Node.js
answer_points: Node.js is an open-source, cross-platform JavaScript runtime environment.
It runs the V8 JavaScript engine outside the browser, providing high performance.
Node.js uses a single-threaded, event-driven architecture with non-blocking I/O.
A simple HTTP server example uses the 'http' module's createServer method.
The server listens on a port and handles requests with request and response objects.
follow_ups: Explain the event loop in Node.js.
What is the difference between CommonJS and ES modules in Node.js?
items.summary: Introduction to Node.js, its architecture, and a basic HTTP server example.

items.question: Running Node.js scripts from the command line
answer_points: Run a Node.js script using 'node app.js'.
Use a shebang line (#!/usr/bin/env node) to make scripts executable directly.
Execute JavaScript code inline with 'node -e "code"'.
Use 'node --watch app.js' to automatically restart on file changes (Node.js v16+).
Use 'node --run <script>' to run scripts defined in package.json.
follow_ups: How do you pass arguments to a Node.js script?
What is the purpose of the --watch flag?
items.summary: Methods to run Node.js scripts, including shebang, inline execution, watch mode, and task runner.
items.source_title: Run Node.js scripts from the command line | Node.js Learn

items.question: Anatomy of an HTTP Transaction in Node.js
answer_points: Create an HTTP server using http.createServer() with a request handler.
Access method, URL, and headers from the request object (IncomingMessage).
Collect request body by listening to 'data' and 'end' events on the request stream.
Set response status code via response.statusCode and headers via response.setHeader().
Send response body using response.write() and response.end(), or pipe the request stream.
Handle errors on both request and response streams to avoid crashes.
follow_ups: How do you handle different HTTP methods and routes?
What is the difference between implicit and explicit headers?
items.summary: Detailed guide on handling HTTP requests and responses in Node.js, including body parsing and error handling.
items.source_title: Anatomy of an HTTP Transaction | Node.js Learn

items.question: Getting file stats in Node.js
answer_points: Use fs.stat() (async) or fs.statSync() (sync) to get file details.
The stats object provides methods like isFile(), isDirectory(), isSymbolicLink().
Access file size in bytes via stats.size.
Promise-based alternative: fs.promises.stat() with async/await.
follow_ups: How do you check if a file exists before reading it?
What is the difference between fs.stat and fs.access?
items.summary: How to retrieve file statistics (type, size) using Node.js fs module.

items.question: JavaScript Asynchronous Programming and Callbacks
answer_points: JavaScript is synchronous and single-threaded by default.
Asynchronicity is achieved via callbacks, Promises, and async/await.
Callbacks are functions passed as arguments to be executed later (e.g., event handlers, timers).
Node.js uses error-first callbacks where the first parameter is an error object.
Callback nesting can lead to 'callback hell'; Promises and async/await are alternatives.
follow_ups: What is callback hell and how do you avoid it?
Explain the difference between callbacks and Promises.
items.summary: Overview of asynchronous programming in JavaScript, focusing on callbacks and their pitfalls.
items.source_title: JavaScript Asynchronous Programming and Callbacks | Node.js Learn

items.question: Introduction to TypeScript
answer_points: TypeScript is a superset of JavaScript that adds static typing.
It helps catch errors early and improves code maintainability.
TypeScript consists of code (with type annotations) and type definitions (.d.ts files).
Type definitions for Node.js are available via @types/node.
TypeScript can transform JSX and modern JavaScript to compatible versions.
follow_ups: How do you set up a TypeScript project with Node.js?
What are the benefits of using TypeScript over JavaScript?
items.summary: Introduction to TypeScript, its components, and how it integrates with Node.js.

items.question: An introduction to the npm package manager
answer_points: npm is the default package manager for Node.js, with over 2.1 million packages.
Use 'npm install' to install all dependencies from package.json.
Install a specific package with 'npm install <package-name>'.
Flags: --save-dev for devDependencies, --save-optional for optionalDependencies.
Update packages with 'npm update'.
npm follows semantic versioning (semver) and supports version constraints.
follow_ups: What is the difference between dependencies and devDependencies?
How do you publish a package to npm?
items.summary: Overview of npm, including installing, updating, and managing packages and scripts.
items.source_title: An introduction to the npm package manager | Node.js Learn

items.question: What is the Diagnostics Working Group and its purpose?
answer_points: The Diagnostics Working Group collaborates with the Node.js Website Team to provide guidance for diagnosing issues in user applications.
The documentation is organized based on user journeys, which are step-by-step procedures to help users root-cause their issues.
follow_ups: How does the user journey approach help in diagnosing issues?
What are some common diagnostic tools provided by Node.js?
items.summary: The Diagnostics Working Group provides guidance for diagnosing application issues through user journey-based documentation.

items.question: Why is testing important in Node.js?
answer_points: Testing verifies that code works as expected and helps catch bugs early in development.
It ensures code reliability and maintainability.
Node.js provides a built-in test runner; refer to the test runner documentation for details.
follow_ups: How do you run tests using Node.js's test runner?
What are the differences between unit tests and integration tests in Node.js?
items.summary: Testing is crucial for code reliability and bug detection; Node.js offers a built-in test runner.
items.source_title: Discovering Node.js's test runner | Node.js Learn

items.question: What are the security best practices for Node.js applications?
answer_points: Use a reverse proxy to handle caching, load balancing, and IP blacklisting to mitigate DoS attacks.
Configure server timeouts (headersTimeout, requestTimeout, timeout, keepAliveTimeout) to drop idle or slow connections.
Limit open sockets per host and total using agent.maxSockets, agent.maxTotalSockets, etc.
Disable the inspector in production and avoid using --inspect in production environments.
Use .npmignore and .gitignore to control which files are published to npm; use npm publish --dry-run to review.
Use constant-time comparison (crypto.timingSafeEqual) for sensitive data to prevent timing attacks.
follow_ups: How does DNS rebinding attack work and how can it be mitigated?
What is HTTP request smuggling and how can it be prevented?
How can you protect against supply chain attacks in Node.js?
items.summary: Security best practices include using reverse proxies, configuring timeouts, limiting sockets, disabling inspector in production, controlling npm publish, and using constant-time comparisons.
